OFOQ | أُفُق

We are a team driven by curiosity, creativity, and a shared passion for technology, innovation, and space exploration.

Our goal for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 is to create OFOQ, an immersive and interactive space mission design game that puts players in the role of mission engineers. Players will design spacecraft, manage resources, make critical decisions, and face unexpected challenges throughout their missions.
summary: Mission Zero is a 3D browser game that turns students into NASA mission engineers. Players walk through a virtual NASA headquarters and run a complete mission to Mars (Jezero Crater) or the Moon's South Pole. They write mission goals, choose instruments, build the spacecraft, pick a real NASA launch vehicle, survive in-flight crises, program the landing, then drive a rover to collect samples. An AI guide, Sadeem, answers questions on demand, but every question lowers the player's independence score.  The game never says "right" or "wrong": physics and NASA open data decide the outcome. Real Mars weather (MEDA/REMS), gravity, solar power, signal delay, launch windows, rocket capacities and LCROSS lunar ice results all drive success or failure. A final report scores five skills and compares the player's design with Perseverance or VIPER.  Space education is mostly read, not experienced. Mission Zero gives students a safe place to make real engineering trade-offs, fail, understand why, and try again. It runs on any phone or laptop with no install. It is Arabic-first with full English support, offers team roles and a teacher dashboard, and makes NASA science accessible to Arabic-speaking classrooms.
details:
Mission Zero is a 3D browser game where the player becomes a NASA mission engineer. It runs in five phases, and each decision carries into the next:

  1. Plan: in the Planning Center, choose Mars (Jezero Crater, search for ancient life) or the Moon's South Pole (search for water ice). Write mission goals, pick science instruments and plan samples. For Mars, choose to wait for the launch window or launch now with reduced rocket capacity.
  2. Build: in the Assembly Hangar, choose power, batteries, thermal control, communications, heat shield, parachute and landing system. Then pick one of five real NASA launch vehicles (Atlas V 401/541, Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, SLS). A live readout compares payload with rocket capacity, fairing size and budget.
  3. Launch & Cruise: a countdown with real stage separation, then timed crises such as solar storms, fuel leaks, computer resets and loss of signal. Because of signal delay, the player must program the landing in advance.
  4. Explore: drive a rover, inspect rocks, collect samples, and manage power and daily data downlink.
  5. Report: a score out of 100 across planning, engineering, crisis management, science return and independence. The report explains each failure and compares the design with Perseverance or VIPER.

Benefits

  • Students learn by doing, and failures are explained so they can try again.
  • The AI guide Sadeem helps on demand through multiple-choice questions, but each question lowers the independence score. This encourages thinking before asking.
  • Side task list, minimap and a skippable tutorial.
  • Arabic-first, with full English support.
  • Runs on phones and laptops, no install.

Intended impact

Make space science hands-on for students, especially Arabic-speaking classrooms where such tools are rare. Teachers can see where a class struggles: in the Claude-hosted version, a teacher dashboard shows class averages, the weakest skill and the most common failure causes, with an AI analysis. Students can also play as a team with three roles: Mission Manager, Rocket Engineer and Mission Scientist.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript (single page)
  • Three.js (r128) for the 3D world, and the Web Audio API for synthesized sound
  • Claude (Anthropic) for Sadeem's answers and the end-of-mission report, through a Node.js serverless function on Vercel that keeps the API key off the client. Built-in answers are used if AI is unavailable.
  • Web Speech API for Sadeem's voice
  • GitHub and Vercel for hosting, and Canva for the presentation
  • Character sprites created from our own videos
  • AI tools also helped us write and test the code

Creativity

  • The game never says "right" or "wrong". Real physics and NASA data decide the outcome, just as in a real mission.
  • An AI mentor you call when you need her, and her help has a cost.
  • Every outcome is compared with a real NASA mission.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific accuracy: every number comes from NASA sources, such as MEDA/REMS weather, planetary constants, signal delay, launch windows, real launch vehicle performance and LCROSS results.
  • Accessibility: Arabic and English, mobile performance, and no install.
  • Learning design: independence over hand-holding, and explained failures.
  • Safety: API keys stay on the server, and the code repository is private
